lines: Every later slice is proven without a bike, a backend or a database. This slice builds what stands in for them.
One shared fixture surrounds the app: a fake Bluetooth stack, answers for the API, and a ride hub that speaks SignalR.
A spec offers a fake bike. Every write the page makes is recorded as hex, and the spec pushes notifications on demand.
Nothing happens unasked. A Bluetooth call the spec did not expect fails it, and the failure names the call.
Requests to the API get the answers the spec declared.
A request nobody answered fails the spec.
The ride hub plays SignalR's JSON protocol: the handshake, then invocations both ways, once the spec opens it.
On the backend, a real SignalR client connects to the API hosted in memory. Without a session, negotiation is refused.
Time moves only when a test moves it: a fake clock in every fixture, and an event probe that waits without sleeping.
Riders see nothing new. Every spec now opens Home inside the doubles, from a phone to a desktop.
What the tests prove: twelve behaviour specs, three proving the guard fails a spec, and eighteen backend tests, all on this machine.
Telo Ride, from the Telo family, turns a smart bike at home into a game.
It pairs with the bike over Bluetooth, reads your power and sets resistance for every hill and interval.

lines.text: Two doors: Race, ride a map against your best-time ghost, bots or people; and Classes, ride along to a video, alone or with a group; fed by one progression of XP, rider levels, stars and map unlocks.
